coachingPoints: Step into the pass with your lead foot — your body weight powers the ball, not your arms alone.
Thumbs down at release keeps the backspin flat and accurate.
Snap the wrists; lazy wrists make lazy, floaty passes that get picked off.
Eyes up — decide your target before the ball arrives, not after.
Passing accuracy matters more than passing speed; aim at the receiver's chest pocket.
commonMistakes: Throwing with straight, stiff arms — no snap, no spin, no control.
Not stepping into the pass — the ball floats and arrives late.
Telegraphing: staring at the target for two seconds before passing — defenders read it.
Passing at the defender's hands instead of leading the teammate away from pressure.
description: The fastest, most accurate way to move the ball — learn the two-hand snap, step, and follow-through.
gameSituations: Skip passes across the court against zone defenses.
Kick-outs from the paint to open shooters.
Full-court outlet passes to start the fast break.

howTo.detail: Catch or hold the ball at chest height, elbows bent and out slightly. Your hands grip the sides of the ball with fingers spread — the classic 'W' thumb position behind the ball.
howTo.title: Start in triple-threat position

howTo.detail: Step toward your target with one foot. This step adds power and gets your momentum moving in the pass's direction.
howTo.title: Step toward the target

howTo.detail: Push the ball straight forward from your chest, extending both arms fully. Your thumbs rotate down at release, putting backspin on the ball so it stays flat and true.
howTo.title: Extend and snap the wrists

howTo.detail: Finish with fingers pointing at the receiver's chest and palms facing out. A full follow-through keeps the pass on a straight line.
howTo.title: Follow through to the target

title: Chest Pass
whatIsIt: The chest pass is basketball's most fundamental throw: a two-handed pass pushed straight from the chest to a teammate's chest. It's the fastest pass to learn, the most accurate over short distances, and the foundation every other pass is measured against.
Because the ball travels in a flat, direct line with backspin, a good chest pass arrives quickly and is easy to catch. It teaches the three pillars of all passing: step, extend, and snap.
whyItMatters: Basketball is won by moving the ball faster than the defense can move. The chest pass is the quickest, most reliable way to do that. Every advanced passing concept — drive and kick, skip passes, pocket passes — assumes you can first make a crisp, accurate chest pass.
